hints.junior: A theme-icon component that only reads `theme` from context lit up on every incoming notification, dozens of times a minute, because it shared one context with the notifications array.
hints.mid: This is exactly how useContext is specified to work: every consumer re-renders when the Provider's value changes, full stop, regardless of which field the consumer actually reads.
hints.staff: React.memo alone won't save a context consumer here, since it still re-renders when the context value's identity changes, that's not the same trigger memo guards against.

hints.junior: This case's demo is a code comparison, not a live toggle, read the broken and fixed versions and follow the comments on which consumers re-render.
hints.mid: The fixed version isn't just 'add more contexts,' notice the useMemo on each provider's value, that's the half of the fix easy to skip.
hints.staff: Watch the note on setter functions, a memoized object with an unstable function inside it still breaks the optimization, memoization has to be structural all the way down.

hints.junior: Give user, theme, and notifications each their own context so a component reading only theme stops re-rendering when notifications changes.
hints.mid: An unmemoized inline value object is a new reference every render of the provider, so every consumer re-renders on every provider render, not just on real state changes, since context compares by reference, not deep equality.
hints.staff: Splitting contexts scopes re-renders by concern, it doesn't give a consumer of one context a way to subscribe to just a slice of that context's value, that needs a selector-based library or a narrower piece of state.

hints.junior: Always wrap a context's value in useMemo with real dependencies listed, not an empty array and not the whole state object out of habit.
hints.mid: useState setters are already stable, use them directly in the memoized value instead of wrapping them in a new inline arrow function, which defeats the memo the same way an unmemoized object would.
hints.staff: Splitting and memoizing doesn't help a consumer that only needs a derived slice of one large, frequently-changing value, track that slice as its own state or reach for a selector-based state library instead.

sections.junior: This case is about a theme icon that kept re-rendering every single time a notification came in, even though it never reads the notifications data at all, just because both lived in the same context.
sections.mid: That's not a bug, it's exactly how useContext is specified to work, every consumer re-renders whenever the provider's value changes, no matter which specific field that consumer actually reads.
sections.staff: React.memo doesn't save you here either, a component still re-renders when its context value's identity changes, that's a different trigger than the prop changes memo is built to guard against.

sections.junior: The fix is giving each piece of unrelated data its own context, so a component reading only the theme stops caring what happens to notifications.
sections.mid: The easy-to-miss half of the fix is memoizing each provider's value, an inline object literal is a brand new reference every render, and context compares by reference, not by what's actually inside it.
sections.staff: Splitting contexts scopes re-renders by concern, but a consumer that only needs a small slice of one still-large context still re-renders on every change to that whole value, that needs a different tool entirely.

sections.junior: This one's a code comparison rather than something to click, read through the broken and fixed versions and follow the comments.
sections.mid: Pay attention to the useMemo call on each provider, adding more contexts without it doesn't actually fix anything.
sections.staff: Notice the callout about setter functions, wrapping a stable setState function in a new arrow function every render quietly breaks the memoization around it.

sections.junior: Every component reading a context re-renders when that context's value changes, even if it only cares about one field that didn't actually change.
sections.mid: Split unrelated data into separate contexts by what changes together, and memoize each provider's value so an unrelated render doesn't create a new object reference.
sections.staff: Memoize all the way down, including setter functions, and reach for a selector-based approach when a consumer needs only a derived slice of one large, frequently-changing value.
